kind.text: I am steady. I am allowed to take up space, and I trust the pace I am moving at today. I do not need to be finished to be worthy of rest. When something is hard, I can slow down, ask for help, and speak to myself as I would to a friend.
Wherever there is a human being, there is an opportunity for a kindness.
kind.author: Seneca

kind.text: You can be patient with yourself the way you are patient with a friend who is learning. You are allowed to go slowly. You are allowed to begin again, and the beginning still counts.

When I catch myself rushing, I can put both feet flat on the floor and finish one thing before starting the next. Hurry is a habit, not a requirement. Today I will do the dishes at the speed of the dishes.

Someone I know is having a harder week than they are saying. I do not need the right words. A short message, a cup of tea left on a desk, a door held open. Today I will pick one person and do one small thing.
Men's minds ought to have relaxation: they rise up better and more vigorous after rest.
kind.author: Seneca

kind.text: I made a mistake at work today. I can name what happened without adding a story about who I am. Then I can fix what can be fixed, apologize once if it is owed, and eat lunch. That is the whole plan.
Stopping for the night is a decision, not a reward. Tonight I will close the laptop at a set time, leave one task undone on purpose, and let tomorrow have it. Pick the time now and write it down.
Regard him as loyal, and you will make him loyal. Some, for example, fearing to be deceived, have taught men to deceive; by their suspicions they have given their friend the right to do wrong.
kind.author: Seneca

kind.text: I talk to myself all day, and most of it is instructions and complaints. For the next hour I will notice the tone. When it turns sharp, I will repeat the sentence in the voice I use with people I like.
If a friend made the mistake I just made, I would not call them careless. I would ask what happened and what comes next. Give yourself the same two questions, and answer them out loud.
Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!
kind.author: The Buddha

kind.text: Having too much to do is a real limit, not a failure of character. The list will not shrink by staring at it. Pick the one item that matters most today, do it, and let the rest wait until tomorrow.

The thought 'I cannot handle this' is a thought, not a report. Notice it, name it, and check what is actually in front of you. Usually it is one email, one call, or one hard conversation. Start with that one.
Let each man direct himself first to what is proper, then let him teach others; thus a wise man will not suffer.
kind.author: The Buddha

kind.text: I cannot control whether the day goes badly. I can control how I treat myself and the people around me while it does. When I feel the urge to snap, I will pause, lower my voice, and say one honest sentence.
Men exist for one another. Teach them then, or bear with them.
kind.author: Marcus Aurelius

kind.text: Find fault with nobody. If you can, set the doer right; if that is impossible, at least set the thing right; if even that cannot be, to what purpose is your fault-finding?
kind.author: Marcus Aurelius

kind.text: Do not be ashamed of being helped. It is incumbent upon you to do your appointed work, like a soldier in the breach. What if you are lame and cannot scale the battlement alone, but can with another's help?
kind.author: Marcus Aurelius

kind.text: If a man mistakes, reason with him kindly and point out his misconception. If you fail, blame yourself, or no one.
kind.author: Marcus Aurelius

kind.text: Kindness is invincible if only it is honest, not fawning or insincere.
kind.author: Marcus Aurelius

kind.text: When any person harms you, or speaks badly of you, remember that he acts or speaks from a supposition of its being his duty. Now, it is not possible that he should follow what appears right to you, but what appears so to himself.
kind.author: Epictetus

kind.text: When, therefore, anyone provokes you, be assured that it is your own opinion which provokes you. Try, therefore, in the first place, not to be hurried away with the appearance.
kind.author: Epictetus

kind.text: If then you wish not to be of an angry temper, do not feed the habit; throw nothing on it which will increase it: at first keep quiet, and count the days on which you have not been angry.
kind.author: Epictetus

kind.text: Ought we then to be angry with them, or to pity them? But show them their error, and you will see how they desist from their errors.
kind.author: Epictetus

kind.text: Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve. The process is mutual; for men learn while they teach.
kind.author: Seneca

kind.text: It helps little to have cast out your own faults if you must quarrel with those of others.
kind.author: Seneca

kind.text: Call to mind what honourable or brave deeds you have done; consider the good side of your own life.
kind.author: Seneca

kind.text: He will not misinterpret a word or a look; he makes light of all mishaps by interpreting them in a generous way.
kind.author: Seneca

kind.text: There remains much more of the road than we have put behind us; but the greater part of progress is the desire to progress.
kind.author: Seneca

kind.text: We must humour our minds and grant them rest from time to time, which acts upon them like food, and restores their strength.
kind.author: Seneca

kind.text: When a man is wandering about our fields because he has lost his way, it is better to place him on the right path than to drive him away.
kind.author: Seneca

kind.text: If anyone is angry with you, meet his anger by returning benefits for it: a quarrel which is only taken up on one side falls to the ground: it takes two men to fight.
kind.author: Seneca

kind.text: We ought not to make our benefits burdensome, or to add any bitterness to them. Even if there be some subject upon which you wish to warn your friend, choose some other time for doing so.
kind.author: Seneca

kind.text: You will make your friend a better man by bearing with him, you will in all cases make him a worse one by reproaching him.
kind.author: Seneca

kind.text: If you had riches, and made other men share them with you, what trouble would you have?
kind.author: Zhuangzi

kind.text: He who knows his stupidity is not very stupid; he who knows that he is under a delusion is not greatly deluded.
kind.author: Zhuangzi

kind.text: He who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot, him I call a real driver; other people are but holding the reins.
kind.author: The Buddha

kind.text: However mean your life is, meet it and live it; do not shun it and call it hard names. It is not so bad as you are. It looks poorest when you are richest. The fault-finder will find faults even in paradise. Love your life, poor as it is.
kind.author: Henry David Thoreau

kind.text: Trust men, and they will be true to you; treat them greatly, and they will show themselves great, though they make an exception in your favor to all their rules of trade.
kind.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

kind.text: Be not hasty, neither speak too loud, nor be too urgent, and so what you desire will be sooner and better accomplished.
kind.author: Plutarch

kind.text: Praise from others must come unasked: we must concern ourselves with the healing of our own lives.
kind.author: Epicurus

kind.text: A short email is not a cold email. My colleague is busy, and so am I. Before I read a tone into three lines, I will answer the question they asked and nothing else.
I will not make this deadline, and pretending otherwise helps no one. Asking for more time is not a confession. Today I will send one clear message with the date I can actually meet.

Lunch at my desk is not lunch. It is eating while working, and I do both worse. Today I will take the full break, leave the phone face down, and taste the food. The emails will keep for thirty minutes.
Someone on my team did the work behind the slide I am about to present. Credit costs me nothing and it is not mine to keep. In the meeting I will say their name and what they did, before anyone asks.

A colleague was short with me last week, and I have carried it since. They probably forgot by dinner. I can set it down without a conversation about it. Tomorrow I will be the one who says good morning first.

My calendar is meetings from nine to five, and by evening I have made nothing I can point to. Unblocking other people is work, and it counts. Before I log off I will write down three things I helped move today.
My mother tells the same story every visit. I can correct her, or I can listen like it is the first time. The story costs me two minutes. Today I will ask one question about it and let her finish.
My child spilled the milk and I raised my voice. That happened. Children learn how to repair from watching us do it. So I will wipe the table, kneel down, and say I am sorry for shouting.
My partner loads the dishwasher wrong, by my rules. The dishes still come out clean. Tonight I will thank them for doing it and keep the correction to myself.
Sitting down while the house is messy is allowed. Nobody is grading the counter. I will set a timer for twenty minutes, sit in the good chair, and do nothing useful until it rings.
I cannot make my father young again or visit every day. I can call on Sunday and mean it. Guilt about what I cannot do steals time from what I can. This week the Sunday call is the whole job.
My brother said something at dinner that stung. He probably did not plan it. I can carry it for a week, or say to him tonight, 'That landed hard, can we talk?' One sentence, then listen.
I am tired, and tired is information, not a judgment on my effort. A worn-out body does not need a lecture about discipline. Tonight I will skip the last chore and turn off the lights by ten.

Being sick is not a failure of willpower. Soup, water, and a blanket are not indulgences; they are the treatment. Today I will cancel what can be cancelled and tell one person plainly: I am unwell and I am resting.

I skipped the run three times this week. The plan was too big for the week I actually had. That is a fact, not a character flaw. Ten minutes of walking still counts. I will put on my shoes and go around the block.

I ate more than I meant to, and now I am arguing with an empty plate. The meal is over. Skipping breakfast as punishment will not undo it. I will drink a glass of water, take a short walk, and eat at the normal time.

Lying awake at 2 a.m. counting the hours left is a second problem stacked on the first. The body still rests when the mind will not. I will turn the clock to the wall and breathe slowly until sleep comes or morning does.

My body did not sign up for the comparison I am running at the gym. It carried me here and it will carry me home. Today I will lift what I can lift, finish the set I planned, and leave when I said I would.

Cooking a real dinner for one is not a waste of effort. I would cook for a guest without a second thought, and tonight I am the guest. I will chop a vegetable, put on some music, and eat sitting down at the table.

I spent more than I planned this month. Calling myself irresponsible does not refund anything. Look at the numbers like a friend doing my books, find the one habit that cost the most, and change that one.

A friend earns more than I do, and I feel the pinch of comparison. Their salary takes nothing from my table. I can be glad for them and mean it. Next time it comes up, I will ask how the new job is going.

I own more than I use. The closet is full and I still feel short. Before I buy anything this week, I will give away one thing someone else needs more. Start with the coat I have not worn in two winters.

I said no to dinner out because money is tight, and felt ashamed saying it. Being careful is not being cheap. My friends would rather have me at a picnic than absent from a restaurant. I will suggest the picnic myself.

The pharmacy line is long, and the woman at the counter is going as fast as she can. Sighing loudly will not move it. I will put the phone away, look at the people around me, and thank her by name when it is my turn.

I am waiting to hear back about the job and I check my inbox every few minutes. Checking is not the same as knowing. Today I will look twice, at noon and at five, and fill the hours between with work I chose.

My friend is late again and I am drafting a speech. The speech will eat the first ten minutes we have together. When they arrive I will say I am glad to see them. If it still matters next week, I will raise it then.

Someone is waiting on a reply from me, and I have been slow. I know how long a silence feels from the other side. I will answer in two lines now, even if the full answer is not ready, and say when it will be.
I am being blamed for something I did not do. Raising my voice will not change what happened. I can state the facts once, calmly, and leave them there. Then I will get back to work.
My colleague and I disagree, and I want to win. Winning would cost me the next ten conversations with them. I will ask what they are worried about, repeat it back, and only then give my view.
I am about to blame someone for the thing that broke. Even if I am right, they already know. Ask what they need to fix it, offer one specific piece of help, and save the postmortem for a calmer day.

pres.text: Right now there is a breath moving through me. I notice the weight of my hands, the sound of the room, the light where it falls. Nothing needs solving in this moment. I am here, and here is enough.
Let not future things disturb thee, for thou wilt come to them, if it shall be necessary, having with thee the same reason which now thou usest for present things.
pres.author: Marcus Aurelius

pres.text: The kettle, the cold floor, the first light on the wall. Ordinary things are not waiting to become something else. I can meet them as they are, one at a time, and let that be the whole task.
Before I open my phone this morning, I will take three slow breaths. Then I will drink a glass of water and feel how cold it is. The day can start after that. Not before.
When I walk to the bus or the car, I will not read on the way. I will count my steps to the corner and listen for the loudest sound and the quietest one. Those two minutes have no other job.
Lay hold of to-day's task, and you will not need to depend so much upon to-morrow's. While we are postponing, life speeds by.
pres.author: Seneca

pres.text: Try this at your desk: feet flat, shoulders down, one long breath out. Then do one task, start to finish, with every other tab closed. When it is done, stand up and stretch before you choose the next one.

Eat one meal today without a screen. Notice the first bite, the temperature, how fast you are chewing. You do not have to eat slowly on purpose. You only have to notice, and let the noticing set the pace.
All difficult things in the world are sure to arise from a previous state in which they were easy, and all great things from one in which they were small.
pres.author: Laozi

pres.text: Something has gone wrong. Before I fix it, I will take one full breath and feel my feet on the floor. Then I will name the actual problem in one sentence and do the first small step.
When it feels like too much, it is usually because I am carrying the whole day at once. I can put the day down. The next ten minutes are all I have to manage, and I can manage ten minutes.
Let us spend one day as deliberately as Nature, and not be thrown off the track by every nutshell and mosquito's wing that falls on the rails.
pres.author: Henry David Thoreau
pres.work: Walden, Where I Lived, and What I Lived For

pres.text: My chest is tight and my thoughts are fast. That is a body under strain, not a verdict on my life. I will unclench my jaw, lower my shoulders, and finish the one task that is already open.
Trouble asks a simple question: what can I do about this right now? If there is something, I do it. If there is nothing, I return to my breath and my work. Either way, the next hour is clear.

You do not have to feel calm to act well. You can be shaken and still wash the cup, send the message, make the call. Steadiness usually follows the hands, not the other way around. Do the small thing first.
Practise attention to what others say, and do your best to get into the speaker's mind.
pres.author: Marcus Aurelius

pres.text: Stick only to the work in hand, and to the tool you have for doing it.
pres.author: Marcus Aurelius

pres.text: Always keep strictly to the first impressions, without adding comments of your own, and you are unaffected.
pres.author: Marcus Aurelius

pres.text: If it is good to use attention to-morrow, how much better is it to do so to-day?
pres.author: Epictetus

pres.text: Every habit and faculty is maintained and increased by the corresponding actions: the habit of walking by walking, the habit of running by running. If you would be a good reader, read; if a writer, write.
pres.author: Epictetus

pres.text: Even bad fortune is fickle. Perhaps it will come, perhaps not; in the meantime it is not. So look forward to better things.
pres.author: Seneca

pres.text: It is indeed foolish to be unhappy now because you may be unhappy at some future time.
pres.author: Seneca

pres.text: Past and future are both absent; we feel neither of them. But there can be no pain except as the result of what you feel.
pres.author: Seneca

pres.text: Hence, every day ought to be regulated as if it closed the series, as if it rounded out and completed our existence.
pres.author: Seneca

pres.text: Whenever a controversy seems likely to be longer or more keenly disputed than usual, let us check its first beginnings, before it gathers strength.
pres.author: Seneca

pres.text: People do not all take offence in the same way; you ought then to know what your own weak point is, that you may guard it with especial care.
pres.author: Seneca

pres.text: The future is not to be waited for; the past is not to be sought again!
pres.author: Zhuangzi

pres.text: If anything is to be done, let a man do it, let him attack it vigorously! A careless pilgrim only scatters the dust of his passions more widely.
pres.author: The Buddha

pres.text: There were times when I could not afford to sacrifice the bloom of the present moment to any work, whether of the head or hands.
pres.author: Henry David Thoreau

pres.text: To finish the moment, to find the journey's end in every step of the road, to live the greatest number of good hours, is wisdom.
pres.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

pres.text: Since our office is with moments, let us husband them. Five minutes of today are worth as much to me, as five minutes in the next millennium. Let us be poised, and wise, and our own, today.
pres.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

pres.text: The utility of living consists not in the length of days, but in the use of time; a man may have lived long, and yet lived but a little. Make use of time while it is present with you.
pres.author: Michel de Montaigne

pres.text: There are forty emails and I can only read one at a time. I read one, answer it or file it, then look at the next. Forty emails is not a wall. It is forty small tasks, and I only ever have to do the one in front of me.

In this meeting I will listen to the person speaking instead of drafting my reply. When my mind runs ahead to my turn, I bring it back to their words. I can decide what to say when they have finished.
The deadline is Friday. It is Tuesday. Friday is not here, and worrying about it does not write a single sentence. I will set a timer for twenty-five minutes and work on the draft until it rings.

A colleague said something sharp and my face is hot. I do not need to reply this second. I feel the heat, I notice the story forming about what they meant, and I give it a full minute before I type anything.
Every notification asks me to be somewhere else. I can turn them off for an hour. My hands on the keyboard, this document, this paragraph. When the hour ends I will check what came in, all at once.
The sink is full again. I can be annoyed about that, or I can feel the warm water and clean one plate. The dishes are not in the way of my evening. For the next ten minutes, they are the evening.
When my partner comes home, I will stop what I am doing before I say hello. Hands empty, eyes up. It costs fifteen seconds. Then I will ask how the day went and listen to the whole answer.
Getting everyone out the door is loud and slow. I will lower my voice instead of raising it. One shoe, one bag, one child at a time. We leave when we leave, and the clock does not need my shouting.

I keep rehearsing what will happen to my father in a year. Today he is in the kitchen making tea and asking about the weather. I will go and sit with him now. The year can ask its questions when they are real.

Before bed I sweep the kitchen floor. Broom, corners, dustpan. It is not really for the floor. It is the line between day and night. When the dustpan is empty, the day is finished and I do not reopen it in bed.

On this run I will not check my pace until the end. I will feel my feet land, hear my breath change on the hill, and notice when my shoulders creep up. If they do, I drop them. The watch can tell me the numbers later.

It is late and I am still scrolling, waiting to feel sleepy. Sleep does not come to a lit screen. I will put the phone in another room, turn off the light, and lie down. Lying still in the dark is enough of a plan.
My back hurts when I sit too long. Pain is my body speaking plainly, and the kind reply is to move, not to be tougher. I will set a timer for forty minutes and stand when it rings, every time.

I slept badly and today will be rougher than I would like. I do not need to make the day good. I need to make it decent: a real breakfast, a short walk at lunch, no big decisions after four. Tomorrow I can try for more.

Look around the room. Most of what you own is doing its job quietly: the chair, the lamp, the mug you always reach for. Before you add anything, find one thing you already own and forgot, and use it today.
In the shop I pick it up and hold it. Do I want the thing, or the feeling of buying? I put it down and walk one more aisle. If my hand still goes back to it, I take it. Most times it does not.

Traffic is stopped and I am not going to arrive on time. That is already true. I send one text to say so and put the phone down. Then I loosen my grip on the wheel and watch the car ahead until it moves.

In the waiting room my name has not been called. My mind is already in the appointment, rehearsing. But I am in this chair, not that room. I feel the chair take my weight and read the poster on the wall, slowly.

I was wrong about the dates and someone has pointed it out. My first urge is to explain. Instead I say, "You are right, thank you," and fix it. Correcting it takes ten seconds. Defending it would take all afternoon.

We disagree and my voice is rising. I notice my hands gripping the edge of the table and loosen them. Then I ask what they would do instead, and I wait for the whole answer. I can disagree at normal volume.

I do not have to correct everyone who is wrong today. Most of these arguments will not matter by Friday. When someone says something I disagree with, I can ask one question, or say nothing, and keep my morning.
After the argument my mind replays it and writes better lines for me. The argument is over. The replays are only thoughts. I notice one, call it "replay", and go back to chopping the onions.

I said the sharp thing and knew it as I said it. I do not need a full account of why I was tired. I walk back into the room and say, "That was unfair. I am sorry." Then I ask what they were trying to tell me.

persp.text: Some things are in our control and others not. Things in our control are opinion, pursuit, desire, aversion, and, in a word, whatever are our own actions.
persp.author: Epictetus

persp.text: Most of what worries me will not matter in a year. I can hold my plans loosely and let the day change them. What is mine to do, I will do. What is not mine, I can set down.
I do not have to force today into the shape I planned. When something will not bend, I can bend instead. I will do the task in front of me, stop when it is done, and let that be enough.
Before I open my inbox, I write down the one thing today needs from me. Everything else can queue behind it. If the list grows, it grows, but that first line does not move.
When a plan falls through, I give myself ten minutes to be annoyed. Then I ask what the afternoon looks like now. Usually there is a smaller, useful thing waiting. I start on that.
Occupy thyself with few things, says the philosopher, if thou wouldst be tranquil.
persp.author: Marcus Aurelius

persp.text: You cannot control the traffic, the weather, or the reply that has not come. You can control when you leave, what you bring, and what you do while you wait. Put your attention there.
At the end of the day I ask two questions. What did I actually do, and what did I only worry about? The second list is usually longer. Tomorrow I move one item from it to the first.
Don't demand that things happen as you wish, but wish that they happen as they do happen, and you will go on well.
persp.author: Epictetus

persp.text: When the meeting moves or the bus is late, I can take the route that is open instead of pushing on the one that closed. Ask what can still happen in the time left, and start there.

Not every message needs an answer today. I read each one, decide if it is urgent, and leave the rest for tomorrow morning. Most of that pile will look smaller by then. Some of it will have solved itself.
How often has the unexpected happened! How often has the expected never come to pass! And even though it is ordained to be, what does it avail to run out to meet your suffering?
persp.author: Seneca

persp.text: Too much is usually many things stacked into one feeling. Write them down. Cross off what is not due today. Cross off what belongs to someone else. What remains is a list, not a weight. Start at the top.

A mistake is information about one thing, not a verdict on the whole day. Name what went wrong in one plain sentence. Fix what can be fixed. Then close the file and give the next task your full attention.
It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full.
persp.author: Laozi

persp.text: Bad news lands harder when I am tired and hungry. Before I decide what it means, I will eat something, drink water, and take ten minutes outside. Then I will look at the problem again and choose one next step.
As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise.
persp.author: The Buddha

persp.text: Do not live as though you had a thousand years before you. The common due impends; while you live, and while you may, be good.
persp.author: Marcus Aurelius

persp.text: Most of the things we say or do are not necessary; get rid of them, and you will gain time and tranquillity.
persp.author: Marcus Aurelius

persp.text: The gourd is bitter: drop it then! There are brambles in the path: then turn aside! It is enough. Do not go on to argue, Why pray have these things a place in the world?
persp.author: Marcus Aurelius

persp.text: If it is not your duty, do not do it: if it is not true, do not say it.
persp.author: Marcus Aurelius

persp.text: Sickness is a hindrance to the body, but not to your ability to choose, unless that is your choice. Lameness is a hindrance to the leg, but not to your ability to choose.
persp.author: Epictetus

persp.text: Be assured, then, that when your own cup likewise is broken, you ought to be affected just as when another's cup was broken. Apply this in like manner to greater things.
persp.author: Epictetus

persp.text: Is anything brought around to you? Put out your hand and take your share with moderation. Does it pass by you? Don't stop it. Is it not yet come? Don't stretch your desire towards it, but wait till it reaches you.
persp.author: Epictetus

persp.text: In every affair consider what precedes and follows, and then undertake it. Otherwise you will begin with spirit; but not having thought of the consequences, when some of them appear you will shamefully desist.
persp.author: Epictetus

persp.text: Do you ask what is the proper limit to wealth? It is, first, to have what is necessary, and, second, to have what is enough.
persp.author: Seneca

persp.text: Recall your steps, therefore, from idle things, and when you would know whether that which you seek is based upon a natural or upon a misleading desire, consider whether it can stop at any definite point.
persp.author: Seneca

persp.text: This is what happens when you hurry through a maze; the faster you go, the worse you are entangled.
persp.author: Seneca

persp.text: All things were ready for us at our birth; it is we that have made everything difficult for ourselves, through our disdain for what is easy.
persp.author: Seneca

persp.text: It is better not to see or to hear everything: many causes of offence may pass by us, most of which are disregarded by the man who ignores them.
persp.author: Seneca

persp.text: If you want to find out the truth about anything, commit the task to time: nothing can be accurately discerned at a time of disturbance.
persp.author: Seneca

persp.text: He who restrains himself within the limits prescribed by nature, will not feel poverty; he who exceeds them will always be poor, however great his wealth may be.
persp.author: Seneca

persp.text: He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent. He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty.
persp.author: Laozi

persp.text: He who lightly promises is sure to keep but little faith; he who is continually thinking things easy is sure to find them difficult.
persp.author: Laozi

persp.text: A pheasant of the marshes has to take ten steps to pick up a mouthful of food, and thirty steps to get a drink, but it does not seek to be nourished in a coop.
persp.author: Zhuangzi

persp.text: But while you cannot regulate yourself, what leisure have you to be regulating the world?
persp.author: Zhuangzi

persp.text: There never was, there never will be, nor is there now, a man who is always blamed, or a man who is always praised.
persp.author: The Buddha

persp.text: Let him not despise what he has received, nor ever envy others: a mendicant who envies others does not obtain peace of mind.
persp.author: The Buddha

persp.text: Victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy. He who has given up both victory and defeat, he, the contented, is happy.
persp.author: The Buddha

persp.text: Not the perversities of others, not their sins of commission or omission, but his own misdeeds and negligences should a sage take notice of.
persp.author: The Buddha

persp.text: Our life is frittered away by detail. An honest man has hardly need to count more than his ten fingers, or in extreme cases he may add his ten toes, and lump the rest.
persp.author: Henry David Thoreau
persp.work: Walden, Where I Lived, and What I Lived For

persp.text: Why should we live with such hurry and waste of life? We are determined to be starved before we are hungry. Men say that a stitch in time saves nine, and so they take a thousand stitches to-day to save nine to-morrow.
persp.author: Henry David Thoreau
persp.work: Walden, Where I Lived, and What I Lived For

persp.text: Shall we always study to obtain more of these things, and not sometimes to be content with less?
persp.author: Henry David Thoreau

persp.text: Do not trouble yourself much to get new things, whether clothes or friends. Turn the old; return to them. Things do not change; we change.
persp.author: Henry David Thoreau

persp.text: Regret calamities, if you can thereby help the sufferer; if not, attend your own work, and already the evil begins to be repaired.
persp.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

persp.text: What I must do is all that concerns me, not what the people think.
persp.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

persp.text: So true is it that nothing is wretched, but thinking makes it so, and conversely every lot is happy if borne with equanimity.
persp.author: Boethius

persp.text: Some fear overmuch what they have strength to bear; others despise overmuch that to which their strength is unequal.
persp.author: Boethius

persp.text: We should not spoil what we have by desiring what we have not, but remember that what we have too was the gift of fortune.
persp.author: Epicurus

persp.text: We must heal our misfortunes by the grateful recollection of what has been and by the recognition that it is impossible to make undone what has been done.
persp.author: Epicurus

persp.text: A deadline moved up, and I want to do everything faster. Instead I ask what the work needs at minimum to be useful. I finish that part well and write one line telling them what comes later.

Someone else took credit for my work. It stings, and then it is over. The work was mine to do and it is done. I will mention my part once, plainly, to the person who needs to know, and then get back to the next piece.
My calendar is full because I said yes to everything last week. Each yes felt small. Today I will decline one meeting I am not needed in and say so in a single sentence.

A colleague is curt in every meeting. I have tried to change that and I cannot. What I can do is state my point clearly, ask a question if I need one, and leave their mood with them when I close the call.

The promotion went to someone else. I wanted it more than I noticed. Before I decide what that means, I list what my job gives me now that I would miss. Then I start today's first task, which has not changed.
The kitchen will be messy again tomorrow. That is not a failure, it is what kitchens do. I wash what is in the sink tonight, wipe the counter, and leave the rest for the morning.
My child's mood is not mine to fix. I can offer a snack, a hug, or some quiet, and then let them have their feelings. Tonight I will listen for two minutes before I try to solve anything.
The plan was a walk in the park. The toddler is asleep in the car. So the plan is now a quiet hour with a coffee in the front seat. I take the hour I was given, not the one I ordered.
Dad will not use the walker no matter how often I ask. His choices are his. Mine are to clear the rug he trips on, keep the hall light on, and call on Sunday like I said I would.

Wanting less can start at the plate. I do not need a second helping to feel finished, I need to notice that I already am. Tonight I serve a smaller portion, eat it slowly, and wait ten minutes before deciding on more.
The bill is the same number whether I dread it or not. Dread just makes me pay it twice. I will open the envelope this morning, write the amount in my budget, and decide what shifts around it.
A raise came and the month still ends tight. Spending grows to fill whatever arrives unless I decide otherwise first. This payday I move a fixed amount to savings before I look at the rest.
Enough is a number, not a feeling. Tonight I write down what a month of my life actually costs. Anything I earn above that line is choice, not need, and I can spend it or keep it on purpose.

A neighbor's new car made mine look shabby overnight. Nothing about my car changed. Before I price anything, I will drive it to work, notice it gets me there, and let that settle the question for this month.

The thing I wanted last year is in a drawer now. That is worth remembering when the next thing looks essential. Before I buy anything over fifty dollars, I wait two nights and see if I still want it on the third morning.

The line moves at the speed it moves. Sighing does not shorten it, and checking the time twice a minute does not either. I have four minutes here, so I answer one message and then put the phone in my pocket.

No reply yet does not mean no. It means they have not replied. I stop inventing their reasons and give it until Thursday. If there is nothing by then, I send one short follow-up and get on with the rest of the week.

Waiting on someone else's decision, I keep rehearsing both outcomes. None of the rehearsals change the result. So I write down what I will do in each case, and today I do the step that is the same in both.

I refresh the tracking page and the package is still in the same city. It will come on the courier's schedule, not mine. I close the tab, decide to check once tonight, and finish the work that is actually in front of me.
The doctor's office is running an hour behind. I can spend that hour annoyed at the receptionist or spend it on the book in my bag. The wait is the same length either way. I pick the book.

Half of the criticism was fair and half was not. I can take the fair half without signing for the rest. I write down the one true point, decide what I will change by Friday, and answer only that part in my reply.

My friend and I will not agree about this, and I have stopped trying to make him. His view is his to hold. I can keep the friendship and lose the argument. Next time it comes up, I will ask about his garden instead.

Someone is angry at me and most of it is not about me. I do not have to catch every word. I listen for the part I can fix, repeat it back so they know I heard it, and let the rest pass without a reply.
